comparison: Perfect agreement on birthdating findings (C15, C25-C41). Both evaluations find the EdU birthdating methodology convincing and well-supported, with OpenEval noting comprehensive data across timepoints and peer reviewers praising the methods as 'convincing' and 'widely used.'

Perfect agreement on spatial mapping analyses (C42-C52). Both evaluations accept the spatial segregation patterns and density contour plots without methodological concerns. Peer reviewers specifically noted attention to cell-type classification differences.

Perfect agreement on the finding that birthdate does not predict motoneuron targeting (C16-C18, C20). Both evaluations support the conclusion that early-born and late-born clades can both be tightly coupled to motoneurons. Peer reviewers noted this discovery will be beneficial for analyzing V1 roles in limb motor circuits.

Perfect agreement on the inference that birthdate alone does not predict functional connectivity (C92). Both evaluations accept this conclusion as well-supported by the data showing diverse connectivity patterns across clades with similar birthdates.

Perfect agreement on background claims (C1-C14). Both evaluations recognize these as well-established literature citations that provide necessary context. Neither raises concerns about these foundational claims.

Strong agreement on discussion/contextual claims (C93-C108, with C57 also in peer R12). Both evaluations accept these as appropriate citations to prior literature that contextualize findings within evolutionary, developmental, and disease frameworks.

Strong agreement on developmental marker expression changes (C53-C56, C58-C60). Both evaluations support the findings on MafB downregulation and developmental changes. Peer reviewers specifically praised attention to differences between current expression and lineage tracing.

Perfect agreement on intersectional genetic labeling findings (C62-C68). Both evaluations support the discrepancy between genetic lineage and protein expression. Peer reviewers explicitly praised this attention to classification differences as addressing a 'frequent source of discrepancy across studies.'

Strong agreement on VGLUT1 synapse analysis and proprioceptive input (C85-C91). Both evaluations accept the methodology and findings showing preferential proprioceptive targeting of specific Foxp2-V1 subgroups. Peer reviewers noted the study 'delves into the connectivity' of these interneurons.

Perfect agreement on Foxp2-V1 molecular subgroups (C80-C84). Both evaluations support the hierarchical classification using Otp and Foxp4 markers. Peer reviewers stated results are 'well supported by data obtained using widely used methods.'

Strong agreement on synaptic connectivity quantification (C71-C79, with peer R4 also covering C69-C70). Both evaluations accept the rigorous 3D reconstruction methodology and findings that Foxp2-V1 and Renshaw cells provide most V1 synapses on motoneuron cell bodies. Peer reviewers highlighted the relatively high proportion of Foxp2-V1 synapses in LMC.

Agreement on technical limitations of circuit tracing (C24). Both evaluations rate as UNCERTAIN due to acknowledged technical limitations including low yield, age-dependent efficiency, and small sample size. OpenEval notes need for additional experiments; peer reviewers note findings are 'suggestive' but 'only a little predictive of function' without direct functional testing.

Partial overlap on reciprocal inhibition role (C22-C23 in OpenEval R12, C23-C24 in peer R8). OpenEval rates C22-C23 as SUPPORTED based on convergent anatomical data; peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, noting that while connectivity is interesting and suggestive, functional involvement requires direct gain/loss of function experiments.

Agreement on segmental distribution findings (C69-C70). Both evaluations support the systematic quantification showing parallel increases in Foxp2-V1s and motoneurons in limb segments. This overlaps with peer R4's broader acceptance of connectivity data including synaptic density patterns.

Agreement on Foxp2-V1 heterogeneity (C19, C21). OpenEval R11 supports heterogeneity through convergent evidence from multiple approaches; peer R6 accepts the molecular subgroup classifications (C21) as well-supported. Both evaluations find the diversity characterization solid.

Agreement on Foxp2-V1 heterogeneity (C19). Both evaluations support this conclusion. OpenEval emphasizes convergent evidence from multiple experimental approaches; peer reviewers praised attention to classification differences that reveal heterogeneity.

Agreement on anatomical placement for reciprocal inhibition (C22). Both evaluations support the anatomical evidence (Otp expression, spatial localization, VGLUT1 synapses). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED; peer reviewers accept anatomical findings but note functional role remains inferential without direct testing.

Minimal overlap on developmental marker changes (C57). OpenEval R3 addresses quantitative immunocytochemistry at P5 vs P0; peer R12 includes C57 among contextual discussion claims. Both accept these findings without concern.
